bai.moTa: The teardrop-shaped light cone, the Hubble sphere, the particle horizon and the event horizon
bai.yChinh: Everything we see lies on our past light cone; drawn in proper distance, the cone is a teardrop at most 5.85 billion light-years wide. The edge of the observable universe (the particle horizon) is now 46 billion light-years away, while a signal we send today can only reach galaxies closer than 16.7 billion light-years (the event horizon). Switch to comoving distance and conformal time, and the light cones straighten out to 45°, just as in flat spacetime.
bai.conSo.1: **13.79 billion years**: the age of the universe (Planck 2018 model, recomputed by this lesson’s code).
bai.conSo.2: **46.1 billion light-years**: today’s distance to the particle horizon, the edge of the observable universe.
bai.conSo.3: **16.7 billion light-years**: the event horizon; a signal sent today will never reach galaxies farther than this.
bai.conSo.4: **14.51 billion light-years**: the radius of today’s Hubble sphere (c/H0).
bai.conSo.5: **5.85 billion light-years**: the widest point of the teardrop-shaped past light cone, at z ≈ 1.6.
bai.conSo.6: **41 million light-years**: the distance, at the time of emission, of the region that emitted the background radiation we see today.
bai.hieuDung: **The Hubble sphere is not the edge of the observable universe.** We still see many galaxies that are receding faster than light (every galaxy with z greater than about 1.5). The real edge is the particle horizon, now 46 billion light-years away.
bai.nguon: Cosmological parameters: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641, A6 (H0 = 67.4; Ωm = 0.315). The three-panel figure and the comparison numbers: Davis and Lineweaver 2004, PASA 21, 97. All numbers in the lesson are computed with src/vat-ly/chan-troi-vu-tru.js and checked in kiem-tra/kiem-vu-tru-4c.mjs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Read a spacetime diagram of the whole universe: the cosmic time axis, the “universe at that moment” slices, and the world lines of galaxies.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Explain why the past light cone is shaped like a teardrop and why we can still see galaxies receding faster than light.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Tell apart the Hubble sphere, the particle horizon and the event horizon, and give today’s value for each.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Convert between proper distance, comoving distance and conformal time, and see the light cones straighten out to 45°.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Read the numbers of the cosmic microwave background: when it was emitted, how far away it was then, and how far away it is now.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: The time axis of the whole universe
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
This is a {{sơ đồ không-thời gian|spacetime diagram}} of the whole observable universe. We (the Milky Way) sit on the central axis; that vertical line is our {{đường thế giới|world line}} and also the time axis. The bottom is the Big Bang. The **green sheet** is today, when the universe is 13.8 billion years old. Above it are the next 25 billion years.

Time here is {{thời gian vũ trụ|cosmic time}}: the number of years since the Big Bang, measured by the clock of someone drifting with the expansion. Every galaxy drifting with the expansion reads the same cosmic age when it measures the same density of the universe, so each **horizontal slice** of the block is “the universe at that moment,” like the “now” sheet in Lesson 4.

The horizontal direction is distance from us. In the first set of axes it is {{khoảng cách thật|proper distance}}: distance measured with rulers laid end to end, right at that moment.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the green dot on the time axis to move “now” up and down: the “now” sheet follows, and the readout shows the age of the universe at that moment. Each small tick you hear while dragging is one billion years passing.
> [[Side view|ngang]] [[Oblique view|toan]] [[Top view|tren]]

> [Lưu ý] The figure drops one dimension of space. The surfaces of revolution have a quarter cut away so you can see the cross-section inside. The time axis is stretched 1.87 times relative to the distance axis for readability (0.28 versus 0.15 scene units per billion years), so in this set of axes light does not travel at 45°. Everything farther than 60 billion light-years is cut off.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
The white lines are the world lines of galaxies drifting with the expansion, in eight directions around us. They all start at the same place at the Big Bang and spread out like a burst of fireworks. The galaxies are not flying through space: the space between them is stretching.

Each galaxy has a constant {{khoảng cách đồng chuyển|comoving distance}} $\chi$ (equal to its proper distance today). Its proper distance when the cosmic time is $t$ is

$$ D(t) = a(t)\,\chi $$

where $a(t)$ is the {{hệ số tỉ lệ|scale factor}} from the Friedmann equation of Lesson 18 ($a = 1$ today). Plugging in numbers: when the universe was 4 billion years old $a \approx 0{,}38$, so a galaxy now 10 billion light-years away was then only 3.8 billion light-years away. In another 25 billion years $a \approx 4{,}4$: it will be 44 billion light-years away.

Look closely at one line: at first it curves in the decelerating way (matter brakes the expansion), then from the time the universe is about 7.7 billion years old it curves in the accelerating way ({{năng lượng tối|dark energy}} takes over).

> [Thử ngay] Drag “now” down to when the universe was about 4 billion years old: the galaxies on the “now” sheet sit closer together, each distance only about 0.38 times today’s, exactly $D = a\chi$.
> [[Show galaxies only|chi]] [[Show all surfaces again|mat]]

+++ Go deeper: the Hubble law from D = aχ
Differentiate with respect to $t$ at constant $\chi$: the recession speed is $v = \dot a\,\chi = (\dot a/a)\,D = H(t)\,D$. That is the Hubble law, valid at every moment with that moment’s $H(t)$. Today $H_0 = 67{,}4$ km/s/Mpc, which means that for every billion light-years of distance, the recession speed grows by $1/14{,}51$ of the speed of light.

The expansion switches from decelerating to accelerating when $\ddot a = 0$, that is $\Omega_m/a^3 = 2\Omega_\Lambda$: $a = (0{,}315/1{,}37)^{1/3} \approx 0{,}61$, corresponding to $z \approx 0{,}63$ and a cosmic age of 7.7 billion years.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
The gold surface is our past {{nón ánh sáng|light cone}} today: the set of all events whose light is reaching our eyes right now. **Everything we see in the sky lies on this surface.** In Lesson 5 the past cone was a straight cone. Here, drawn in proper distance, it bulges out and then closes in again into a **teardrop**, at most 5.85 billion light-years wide, at redshift $z \approx 1{,}6$, when the universe was 4.1 billion years old.

Why? Light always travels at speed $c$ relative to the space right where it is, but that space is receding from us. The proper distance from the light ray to us changes as

$$ \frac{\dd D}{\dd t} = H\,D - c $$

When $H D \gt c$, the ray, although aimed at us, is still carried farther away. Only when the expansion slows and $H D$ drops below $c$ can the ray start getting closer.

> [Thử ngay] Choose the galaxy at $z = 3$: its light left it when it was 5.3 billion light-years from us, was first pushed out to 5.85 billion light-years, and only then turned back, taking 11.7 billion years. Drag the pink dot (the selected galaxy) along the “today” sheet: the gold ray and the bright dot running along it show when and where the light we receive today left the galaxy.
> [[Zoom in on the teardrop|giot]] [[Galaxy at z = 3|z3]] [[Galaxy at z = 1|z1]]

+++ Go deeper: from dχ = −c dt/a to the teardrop
Light heading toward us covers a proper distance $c\,\dd t$ in each interval $\dd t$, that is, a comoving distance $c\,\dd t/a$. Integrating from emission to today: $\chi = \int c\,\dd t/a = \eta_0 - \eta(t)$, where $\eta$ is conformal time (step 7). The proper distance at emission is $D = a\,(\eta_0 - \eta)$.

As $a \to 0$, $D \to 0$; when $a = 1$, $\eta = \eta_0$ and $D = 0$. In between, $D$ must reach a maximum, exactly where $\dd D/\dd t = 0$, that is $H D = c$: the widest point of the teardrop lies on the Hubble sphere of the next step.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Drag the galaxy to where the light we receive today left it exactly when it was **farthest from us**, at the widest point of the teardrop: an emission distance of 5.82 billion light-years or more.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: The widest point of the teardrop is at $z \approx 1{,}6$: a galaxy now about 15 billion light-years away. Read the “distance at emission” line on the galaxy card.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: The Hubble sphere: where recession equals c
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The blue surface is the {{mặt cầu Hubble|Hubble sphere}}: the places where the recession speed $v = H D$ equals $c$. Its proper radius is $c/H(t)$; today

$$ \frac{c}{H_0} = \frac{977{,}8}{67{,}4} \approx 14{,}51\ \text{tỉ năm ánh sáng} $$

Galaxies outside this sphere recede **faster than light**. That does not contradict special relativity: special relativity only forbids outrunning light **locally**, compared with a light ray passing the same place. Recession speed is the rate at which distance grows, added up over a large region of space, not the speed of an object relative to the space around it.

And we still see many such galaxies. Every galaxy with $z \gt 1{,}48$ is receding faster than $c$ today. The galaxy at $z = 3$ was receding at $1{,}67\,c$ when it emitted, and recedes at $1{,}46\,c$ now, yet its light is reaching us.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “A galaxy receding faster than light can never be seen; the Hubble sphere is the edge of the observable universe.” Wrong. Davis and Lineweaver (2004) point out that this is one of the most common confusions, even in textbooks. The real edge is the particle horizon (next step).

> [Thử ngay] Drag the galaxy back and forth across the edge of the Hubble sphere on the “today” sheet: a small note sounds each time it crosses.
> [[Galaxy at z = 3|z3]] [[Galaxy at z = 1.48|z148]] [[Galaxy at z = 0.5|z05]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the galaxy to where, when it emitted the light we receive today, it was receding at **twice the speed of light** ($2\,c$, to within $0{,}08\,c$). That light still reaches us.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: The galaxy at $z = 3$ was receding at $1{,}67\,c$ at emission; you need to go a bit farther: around $z \approx 3{,}8$, now about 23 billion light-years away.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: The particle horizon: edge of the observable universe
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
The pale violet surface is the {{chân trời hạt|particle horizon}}: the farthest place from which light emitted at the Big Bang has had time to reach us by that moment. Today it is

$$ \chi_{\text{hạt}} = \int_0^{t_0}\frac{c\,\dd t}{a(t)} \approx 46{,}1\ \text{tỉ năm ánh sáng} $$

away, even though the universe is only 13.8 billion years old. There is no contradiction: while the light was traveling, the path it had already covered kept stretching behind it. This edge is now receding at about $3{,}2\,c$.

The particle horizon grows with time: every year that passes, light from farther regions has had time to arrive. The cosmic microwave background was emitted from a sphere now 45.2 billion light-years away, just inside the particle horizon; the rest is light from the first 371,000 years, when the universe was still opaque and could not be seen through.

> [Thử ngay] Drag “now” into the past: the particle horizon was closer then, because light had not yet had time to travel far; galaxies outside it were “not yet visible.”
> [[Zoom out to the full view|toan]] [[Galaxy at z = 11|z11]] [[Background radiation z = 1090|z1090]]

+++ Go deeper: comparison with Davis and Lineweaver 2004
For their model ($H_0 = 70$; $\Omega_m = 0{,}3$; $\Omega_\Lambda = 0{,}7$; radiation neglected), this lesson’s code gives an age of 13.5 billion years, a particle horizon of 46.2 billion light-years and an event horizon of 15.9 billion light-years; the paper quotes a particle horizon of 46 billion light-years and an event horizon of 16 billion light-years. For the Planck 2018 model used here: age 13.79 billion years, particle horizon 46.1 billion light-years, event horizon 16.7 billion light-years. The two models differ in $H_0$ and $\Omega_m$, so the numbers differ by only a few percent.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: Drag “now” into the past until the edge of the observable universe is only **half** as far as today: the particle horizon at 23 billion light-years (proper distance, to within 1).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: Hover over the green dot to read the distance to the particle horizon. The target is around the time the universe was 7.6 billion years old.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: The event horizon: signals that never arrive
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
The red-orange surface is the universe’s {{chân trời sự kiện|event horizon}}; the faint gold surface opening upward is our **future** light cone today: the path of a signal we send right now. Because the expansion is accelerating, that signal, however long it travels, can only reach galaxies with comoving distance less than

$$ \chi_{\text{sk}} = \int_{t_0}^{\infty}\frac{c\,\dd t}{a(t)} \approx 16{,}7\ \text{tỉ năm ánh sáng} $$

that is, galaxies with $z \lt 1{,}87$. Conversely, light that farther galaxies emit **today** will never reach us. We still see them, but only their past, and that image will grow redder and fainter forever.

The event horizon is different from the particle horizon: the particle horizon asks “**has** the light reached us yet?”, the event horizon asks “**will** the light ever reach us?” In the long run the proper radius of the event horizon approaches $c/(H_0\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda}) \approx 17{,}5$ billion light-years.

> [Thử ngay] In the comoving axes, the signal’s path creeps ever closer to the vertical line $\chi = 16{,}7$ without touching it.
> [[Galaxy at z = 1.87 (right at the edge)|z187]] [[Galaxy at z = 1|z1]] [[View in comoving distance|he2]] [[Back to proper distance|he1]]

> [Lưu ý] The sound is translated so the ear can hear it. While you drag a galaxy, the sustained tone has pitch $660/(1 + z)$ Hz: the farther away, the more its light reaching us is stretched and the lower the tone. Crossing outside the event horizon plays a low note (from then on, contact is lost forever); coming back inside plays a bright note.

> [Lưu ý] The figure 16.7 depends on whether dark energy stays the same forever. The model here assumes it is a cosmological constant. DESI data (2024–2025) hint that dark energy may be weakening over time, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to be conclusive.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Drag the galaxy **just outside** the event horizon: we still see it today, but the light it emits today will never reach us. Target: a comoving distance 0.2 to 1.3 billion light-years beyond the edge.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: The edge is at 16.7 billion light-years ($z \approx 1{,}87$). Drag outward until you hear the low note and the galaxy card says “Outside the event horizon,” then stop before 18 billion light-years ($z \approx 2{,}1$).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: Changing axes: the light cones straighten
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Click the three sets of axes in turn. The figure morphs smoothly from one to the next; no event is lost.

1. **Proper distance × cosmic time**: the picture you have seen so far.
2. **Comoving distance × cosmic time**: divide every distance by $a(t)$. Galaxy world lines become **vertical lines**; the teardrop opens into a funnel.
3. **Comoving distance × conformal time**: also change the time axis to $\eta$ with $c\,\dd\eta = c\,\dd t/a$. Now light travels along $\dd\chi = \pm c\,\dd\eta$: **every light ray is tilted at exactly 45°**, as in Lesson 5.

In axes 3, our past cone is a straight cone; the event horizon is an **upside-down** 45° cone with its apex at $\eta_\infty = 62{,}8$ billion years, the top edge of the figure (the whole infinite future squeezed into a finite height); the particle horizon is the 45° cone rising from us at the Big Bang. The causal structure can be read by eye, just as in flat spacetime.

> [Thử ngay] In axes 3, drag “now” into the future: our 45° past cone widens, creeping up on the upside-down event-horizon cone but never crossing it.
> [[Proper distance|he1]] [[Comoving|he2]] [[Comoving + conformal|he3]]

+++ Go deeper: why it is called “conformal”
The metric of a flat universe is $\dd s^2 = -c^2\dd t^2 + a(t)^2(\dd\chi^2 + \chi^2\dd\Omega^2)$. Substitute $c\,\dd t = a\,c\,\dd\eta$:

$$ \dd s^2 = a(\eta)^2\left[-c^2\dd\eta^2 + \dd\chi^2 + \chi^2\dd\Omega^2\right] $$

Inside the square brackets is the flat metric of Lesson 5. The factor $a^2$ in front scales all distances equally in every direction, so it does not change the angles between directions (“angle-preserving,” in English: conformal). Light cones ($\dd s = 0$) are therefore exactly the same as in flat spacetime.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: The cosmic microwave background: the most distant picture
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
The ring near the bottom is the **last scattering surface**, where the {{bức xạ nền vi sóng vũ trụ|cosmic microwave background}} was emitted: the oldest light we receive. The lesson’s model computes:

| Quantity | Computed value |
|---|---|
| Redshift | $z = 1090$ |
| Age of the universe at emission | 371,000 years (books usually round to 380,000) |
| Proper distance at emission | 41 million light-years |
| Distance today | 45.2 billion light-years |
| Light travel time | 13.79 billion years |
| Recession speed at emission / today | $66\,c$ / $3{,}1\,c$ |

At emission, that region was only 41 million light-years from the place that would later become the Milky Way, yet it was already receding at 66 times the speed of light; the light took almost the entire age of the universe to escape the flow of expansion and reach us. Since then the distance has stretched by exactly $1 + z = 1091$ times.

> [Tóm lại] Age of the universe 13.79 billion years; $c/H_0 = 14{,}51$; event horizon 16.7 billion light-years; particle horizon 46.1 billion light-years. The past cone is at most 5.85 billion light-years wide, at $z \approx 1{,}6$. In comoving and conformal axes, everything returns to the 45° cone geometry of Lesson 5.

[[Background radiation z = 1090|z1090]] [[Proper axes|he1]] [[Conformal axes|he3]]
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: $c\,\eta$ is the comoving distance light has traveled since the Big Bang.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: $\chi$ is constant for a galaxy drifting with the expansion; $v$ is the recession speed.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: Units: billion light-years. Today’s Hubble sphere: $c/H_0 = 14{,}51$.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: A galaxy at z = 3 is receding from us today at about 1.46 c. Can we see it?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: No, because it recedes faster than light
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: Yes: the light it emitted when the universe was 2.1 billion years old is reaching us
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.3: Only if it lies inside the Hubble sphere
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.4: No, because it lies outside the particle horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: Whether we can see it is decided by the particle horizon (46.1 billion light-years), not by the Hubble sphere. The galaxy at z = 3 is now 21.2 billion light-years away, inside the particle horizon. Its light was first carried away and only then turned back, taking 11.7 billion years.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Roughly what is today’s radius of the observable universe (the particle horizon)?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.1: 13.8 billion light-years, because the universe is 13.8 billion years old
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: The light traveled for 13.8 billion years, but the path behind it stretched in the meantime, so the source is now 46 billion light-years away. 14.5 is the radius of the Hubble sphere, a different concept.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: Light from a galaxy at z = 11 left that galaxy when it was how far from us (proper distance at emission)?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: The proper distance at emission is $a(\eta_0 - \eta)$: 2.7 billion light-years, because the universe was still small then ($a = 1/12$). 32 is the distance today; 13.4 is the time the light has traveled (in billions of years), not a distance.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Today we send a radio signal to a galaxy that is now 20 billion light-years away. Will the signal arrive?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: Yes, we just have to wait 20 billion years
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: Yes, but we have to wait longer than 20 billion years
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.3: Never, because 20 is larger than the event horizon of 16.7
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.4: No, because it is outside the Hubble sphere
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: A signal sent today can only reach galaxies with comoving distance below 16.7 billion light-years. Being outside the Hubble sphere (14.5) is not enough to decide: a galaxy at 15 billion light-years still receives it, though very late.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: In comoving distance × conformal time axes (with the same scale), at what angle to the time axis does a light ray travel?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: Exactly 45°, everywhere and at all times
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: Less than 45° when the universe was young
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.3: More than 45° outside the Hubble sphere
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: Conformal time is defined so that $\dd\chi = \pm c\,\dd\eta$ for every light ray. The metric differs from the flat metric only by a common factor $a^2$, so the light cones are just as in Lesson 5.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Why, if the universe is only 13.8 billion years old, can we see places that are now 46 billion light-years away? Explain using the spacetime diagram.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Light comes to us along the past light cone. Along the way, at each place it travels at speed $c$ relative to the local space, but the stretches of path it has already covered keep expanding with $a(t)$. Adding up all those stretches in terms of today’s distances gives $\chi = \int c\,\dd t/a = 46{,}1$ billion light-years, more than $c \times 13{,}8$ billion years because $a \lt 1$ throughout the past. In the comoving × conformal diagram this shows directly: our 45° past cone meets the bottom (the Big Bang) at $\chi = c\,\eta_0 = 46{,}1$.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: T. M. Davis and C. H. Lineweaver, “Expanding Confusion,” PASA 21, 97 (2004): the three-panel spacetime figure this lesson rebuilds, and the misconceptions about recession speed and horizons.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: B. Ryden, *Introduction to Cosmology* (2nd ed., 2016): proper distance, comoving distance, the particle horizon and the event horizon.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapters 17–18: cosmology, the FRW metric, conformal diagrams.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641, A6: the cosmological parameters used in the lesson.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: Time since the Big Bang, measured by the clock of someone drifting with the expansion. Each slice of constant cosmic time is “the universe at that moment.”
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: The quantity $\eta$ with $c\,\dd\eta = c\,\dd t/a(t)$. Using it as the time axis and comoving distance as the space axis makes every light ray tilt at 45°.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: Distance measured with rulers laid end to end at a single moment of cosmic time. Equal to $a(t)$ times the comoving distance.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The set of events whose light reaches an observer at a given moment. Everything we see in the sky lies on our past light cone.
